questions.prompt: A city has two hospitals: Large Hospital delivers 45 babies daily, Small Hospital delivers 15. Over one year, each hospital records the days when more than 60% of births were boys. Which hospital likely recorded more such days?

choiceExplanations.Cannot be determined from the informatio: Statistical theory of sampling variability is sufficient to predict which hospital sees more extreme days; no additional information is needed.

questions.prompt: A medical test for a rare disease (1 in 1000 prevalence) is 99% accurate: it correctly identifies 99% of sick people and 99% of healthy people. If you test positive, what is the approximate probability you actually have the disease?
questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem: P(disease|+)=(0.99×0.001)/[(0.99×0.001)+(0.01×0.999)]≈0.00099/0.01098≈9%. The very low base rate (1/1000) generates far more false positives than true positives.

choiceExplanations.About 99%: Ignores the base rate entirely; among 100,000 people there are ~99 true positives but ~999 false positives, so 99% is far too high.
choiceExplanations.About 50%: 50% would require roughly equal true and false positives, which needs ~50% prevalence, not 1/1000.
choiceExplanations.About 1%: 1% is close to the prior base rate alone and fails to account for the updating power of a positive test result.
choiceExplanations.About 9%: Correct Bayesian calculation: the rare prevalence swamps test accuracy, leaving only about a 9% chance of true disease after a positive result.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 30 red and 70 blue marbles. You draw one marble, note its color, return it, and draw again. Given that at least one draw was red, what is the probability both draws were red?
questions.explanation: P(both red)=0.3²=0.09; P(at least one red)=1−0.7²=0.51; conditional probability=0.09/0.51≈17.6%≈18%. The condition 'at least one red' restricts the sample space, raising the probability above the unconditional 9%.

choiceExplanations.About 9%: 9% is the unconditional probability of two red draws (0.3²), ignoring the conditioning event.
choiceExplanations.About 30%: 30% is the probability of a single red draw on one trial, not the conditional probability requested.
